It is always disappointing when a universally acclaimed film fails to connect, but few cinematic letdowns are quite as exhausting as Harakiri. The pacing is excessively slow, and I never cared enough about the characters for the gradual revelations to have much impact. Yes, some of the shots are beautiful, but attractive cinematography can only carry a film so far. Much of the film consists of long conversations and information being revealed piece by piece. Instead of building tension, this made the experience increasingly frustrating. By the time the narrative finally becomes genuinely engaging, there are only about 20 minutes left. The core drama effectively feels delayed until the final stretch. Considering its reputation as a masterwork, I expected something far more compelling. I genuinely struggle to understand how anyone could call it an exceptional film. A handful of strong scenes does not automatically make a great movie, especially when getting to them feels like such a chore.

A rewatch has set in, and after a late reconsideration, I'm quite convinced this film is borderline mediocre. My previous review was based on a very guided perspective, but honestly, I don't think this film is impressive in any particular regard, especially in the areas it should excel in, given that they're its focal points. Storytelling, its narrative progression, character portrayal, characterization, and its supposed thematic depth. to give it some grace, perhaps the narrative progression could have been seen as monumental at the time. However, the storytelling is unbelievably mediocre and questionable. I've seen still images with more interesting details. As for its supposed thematic depth and philosophical questions, they're presented so openly that I genuinely think the film's ideas could have been much more easily consumed in a book than in a movie with a three hour runtime. I know I previously praised the film, and that praise still stands to an extent. However, I'm seeing so many insufferable opinions about it, almost as if no high school movie does actually possess more depth than this it. It's an okay film at best. It's a good talking point, but it's not worth three hours of your life. There's no particularly deep conceptual or philosophical work at play here. No, you cannot write a thousand word essay on this film without stretching its ideas beyond what they actually offer. You can effectively encapsulate its entire purpose and thematic depth in two sentences, and the other person would hardly have missed anything. In fact, you'd probably be overinforming them. people will overlook genuine filmmaking errors that take away from what a film could have been, but because it was made three hundred years before Christ was born, and the director is Japanese, lost an arm and a leg in the war, and are subsequently tripped into watching it, people seem to believe they're obligated to regard it as elite filmmaking. No. That's not how it works.

Harakiri is a Japanese film about something uniquely Japanese. Outside of Japan, Western Internet culture has completely glamorised the samurai. To a certain brand of anime fan, the samurai are the definitive proof that anything Japanese is inherently cooler than anything else. And yet, if you ask these same people about their own country's history, they are suddenly deeply sceptical. How can they be so certain that a foreign country's culture is so flawless, despite never having grown up there - let alone ever visited? The truth is, a country's cultural exports are in no way indicative of what life there is actually like. Take the royal family, for example. Supposedly, the British aristocracy is beloved globally. The King’s Speech , Downton Abbey, royal weddings - if it’s about the British upper class, the rest of the world can't get enough of it. But if you actually ask those of us who live here what we think of Buckingham Palace, the King's Christmas speech, or the endless millions spent on coronations... for at least half of the country, the answer might surprise you. Look at the American frontier. It has been endlessly romanticised as the rugged, iconic image of the United States. But ask an actual American historian, and they’ll explain exactly why it was called the "Wild" West. These cultural exports are just a façade. They're propaganda. They're nothing more than the way an establishment brands, packages, and sells its history to bring in tourists. That is all they're for. Harakiri , written by Shinobu Hashimoto, uses the samurai’s iconic status to tear down that exact kind of propaganda. It examines bushido - the samurai’s so-called moral code - with a far more critical eye than a Western audience might expect. The word façade is spoken several times in the script, and that is the core theme of the film. Bushido wasn't a noble moral code, it was a hypocritical lie maintained by the establishment to protect its own status quo. The film makes this point so clearly that by the third act, the characters are practically arguing these ideas out loud. Because of that, it's absolutely essential viewing if you want to actually learn about Japan, rather than just consume its popular culture. But... I don't think it has much rewatch value. The film relies on a non-linear plot. Crucial information is only revealed when it will have the absolute maximum dramatic impact. Watching it for the first time is like listening to a great joke. But once you've heard the joke, you already know the punchline. When I watched it again, the magic faded. I was just sitting there, waiting for the reveal. It's like sketch comedy. Once you’ve seen the character's gimmick, you know their catchphrase. The plot structure of Harakiri relies so heavily on those massive structural twists that during my second watch, the tension was gone. The first time, I was fully engaged because I was several steps behind the narrative, enjoying the thrill of catching up. The second time, I was several steps ahead, just waiting for the movie to catch up to me. It’s a brilliant trick, but it's a trick that only works once. I highly recommend it to anyone who hasn't seen it yet. But for me, it’s not a film I can see myself returning to over and over.

Letterboxd, for me, is a place for honesty. In that vein, Harakiri was not all that special to me, though I so wanted it to fulfill the countless reviews lavishing praise on this movie. Sure, it’s plotting was clever and seamless, sure, there were scenes of tremendous beauty, and, sure, Tatsuya Nakadai gave a stellar lead performance, but, on the whole, this film never captured me, indeed, it often bored me. Maybe this can be attributed to environmental factors (I was tired and warm), yet still, for a real masterpiece it wouldn’t have mattered a lick. And this isn’t just some bog standard “it’s slow and black and white” sort of critique—I enjoyed Satantango —it’s just the case that for all its drama and ornate storytelling I was never bought into this movie. Roger Ebert once said what makes movies so special is their unique ability to immerse the viewer, more than any other art form can, and make them forget about all the little troubles of daily life (e.g., getting home from the theater). Unfortunately, Harakiri entirely failed on this count (all I could think about the last hour was getting the BART home). Still, I’m happy, at least, to cross this classic off the list, and I look forward to more Kobayashi at BAMPFA soon. 3/5.

I've finally set aside some time to engage with the commotion surrounding this film, and I have a few things I'd like to address.Firstly, credit where credit is due. I think the film does a commendable job of establishing its narrative foundations, gradually revealing the circumstances behind its central conflict and the motivations that drive Tsugumo. At its core, this is a story about a man whose relationship with honour has become increasingly complicated by his responsibilities as a father, a friend, and a samurai. As his circumstances deteriorate and his losses accumulate, we witness the psychological burden of a man struggling to reconcile his personal values with the expectations imposed upon him by the society he inhabits. His guilt is palpable, and the film succeeds in making his internal conflict somewhat telling. The acting, in particular, is well executed.However, my appreciation for the narrative does not necessarily translate into an appreciation for the film as a cinematic experience. For me, the pacing is one of its most significant shortcomings. A story whose central conflict can be understood relatively early takes over two hours to unfold, and I struggle to justify the amount of time devoted to it. While the gradual revelation of information serves a clear narrative purpose, I don't believe the execution consistently warrants its runtime.Furthermore, I find it difficult to evaluate the film independently of its historical and cultural context. Understanding the director's intentions, alongside the social structures and conceptions of honour that inform the narrative, undoubtedly betters the experience. Nevertheless, I don't believe contextual significance should automatically elevate a film's artistic merit. Without that additional understanding, I struggle to see it exceeding a 6/10, or three stars.My reservations extend to the cinematography. I found the camera work relatively uninspiring for large portions of the film, with angles and compositions that rarely generated the emotional resonance or visual atmosphere I look for in filmmaking. Consequently, the film relies heavily on its writing and performances to sustain my engagement. Fortunately, the acting delivers, giving the narrative much of the weight that I feel its visual presentation lacks.As for rewatchability, I see very little. I have no particular desire to revisit this film, even if my memory of it were erased. That isn't to suggest that it's a bad film, nor that I failed to understand what it was trying to communicate. Rather, I simply don't believe its strengths outweigh its shortcomings enough to justify another viewing.

I don't know if I'm missing something when I say that what is often considered one of the greatest films ever made, I found extremely boring. I don't think I've yet found a samurai film that I've liked and, aside from Toshio Matsumoto's Demons , Harakiri is no exception. I think the main issue I had with the film was just how long winded it was, being essentially that this is just the main character giving one long speech. If I go back to Demons , that works as a samurai revenge film because there is a clear dichotomy between exploitation of the main character, being robbed by a geisha, and his reason for revenge ('you messed with me, now prepare to die.') With Harakiri , in so executing a weaving narrative, though I understand completely what Kobayashi was going for, it feels as though it’s trying too hard to understand samurai rituals metaphysically, and it just ends up turning into into 'shut up and kill yourself already.' I will say though there are parts of this film that look absolutely stunning, and on the whole it is a very pretty film, Kobayashi is certainly a director worthy of praise. It’s just a shame that the clear introspectiveness the film tries to present is to me very dull.

١٠/١٠ - The third movie in our recommendation series, and today’s pick is Harakiri ! One of the movies I’ve been looking forward to watching the most, but at the same time, I was kinda hesitant because I wasn’t sure if I’d actually enjoy it. I kept seeing so many people putting it in their top 4, and it’s literally ranked as the #1 movie on Letterboxd, so that alone got me even more excited. And honestly, all that hype was NOT for nothing. What an absolute masterpiece. The fact that this movie came out 64 years ago and still manages to be better than so many movies coming out today is insane!! This movie has SO many things going for it, and honestly, it’s easy to see why it’s considered one of the greatest films in cinema history. The screenplay is easily one of the strongest aspects of the movie. This is exactly the kind of film that reminds you how important good writing is. It’s so clever and well put together, and instead of following a straightforward beginning-to-end narrative, it slowly reveals its story piece by piece. The more you learn, the more your perspective on the characters and everything that’s happening changes . And the way the flashbacks are used to connect the past with the present without making the story feel confusing is just brilliant. Now let’s talk about the direction. This was my first Masaki Kobayashi movie, and damn, he really proved himself to be an incredible director. He delivered an absolutely phenomenal piece of filmmaking. Using the simplest things, from camera angles to camera movements and composition, he managed to create so much tension and keep you hooked. Every single shot feels carefully thought out. Sure, there are some slower moments, but they all serve a purpose, and you’ll understand why as the story unfolds. 🚨 SPOILERS AHEAD, SO DON’T KEEP READING IF YOU HAVEN’T SEEN THE MOVIE 🚨 This movie is PACKED with amazing ideas and deep philosophical messages, and one of my favorites is the whole idea of real honor vs. fake honor . So, what do I mean by that? The Ii clan constantly talks about their traditions and honor, and sees itself as the protector of the samurai code. But when Motome, a poor samurai struggling to survive, shows up asking to perform seppuku in their courtyard, what do they do? Instead of treating him with dignity and showing him some compassion, they take advantage of his situation and force him into an extremely humiliating death. He even asks them to give him two days before carrying out the ritual, but they completely refuse and humiliate him instead. But why? Because back then, many samurai had lost their masters and fallen into poverty. Some would visit wealthy clans pretending they wanted to commit seppuku, hoping the clan would take pity on them, spare their lives, and give them some money. So the Ii clan decided to make an example out of Motome. They wanted to send a message to anyone who tried pulling the same trick: if you come here asking for seppuku, we’ll make sure you go through with it, whether you’re serious or just desperate for money. But how can a clan that constantly talks about honor and tradition humiliate someone and take advantage of his suffering in the name of protecting those very traditions? Like, what exactly is so honorable about that? All they care about is maintaining their reputation and protecting their image, not human lives. And that’s what makes their idea of honor so fake. And then there’s Hanshiro, who came to them asking for the same thing, yet turned out to be the one person who truly understood what honor actually means. He cared about human dignity, stood up for the truth, was willing to sacrifice himself, and refused to accept injustice. Everything the Ii clan claimed to stand for, he actually embodied. And THE ENDING… DAMNNNN. Putting the fight aside, which almost felt like a theatrical performance, the moment Hanshiro destroys the armor was absolutely incredible. Those armors represented the clan’s power, prestige, and history. By destroying them, it was almost as if he was telling them: You keep talking about honor and traditions, but you have absolutely no real honor. It’s all just a facade. And when they finally kill Hanshiro because they can’t let him walk away after exposing everything about them, they go on to rewrite the entire story to protect their reputation. What actually happened was that Hanshiro killed three of their samurai and wounded several others, and the clan killed him to silence him. Motome was also forced into a humiliating death . But what did the clan tell everyone? They claimed the three samurai died of illness. Instead of admitting that they killed Hanshiro, they recorded his death as a proper ritualistic seppuku, making it look like he died according to their traditions. And they did the same with Motome’s story. They basically rewrote everything to make themselves look honorable and preserve their reputation. In the end, what an absolute cinematic masterpiece. Definitely deserves to be among the greatest films on Letterboxd, but does it deserve the number one spot? Honestly, no . “What befalls others today, may be your own fate tomorrow.” What a fantastic movie. I guess it’s position at no.1 on Letterboxd’s best movies list should’ve tipped me off, but damn, I was nowhere near prepared for the journey this one took me on. There is a certain mythology surrounding the Samurai. The “live by the sword, die by the sword” mentality of honour is oft misinterpreted, and misunderstood as a truly virtuous or heroic way to live. In actuality, the Samurai were a vicious and brutal ruling class, a tool of empire, and their traditions haunted an entire society for years. Can you imagine being told the only recourse to failure is to gut yourself before your peers? Now look, I love a good Samurai movie, in all their inaccuracies. But what I love more , is a movie that deconstructs the Samurai and the era surrounding them, and it’s done fantastically here. It’s a movie that tells its story so perfectly that, if it were made today, I doubt anything would change in how it goes about its plot. There’s nothing you can add or develop on more: it’s absolutely, timelessly perfect. Tsugumo is a protagonist who I immediately was enraptured by. His story explores the class divide of the Edo period, as well as ideas of revenge, honour, and retribution in incredible fashion. To expect anything less of a fantastic performance from Tatsuya Nakadai would be foolish, and he delivers one of his best here. In his intense back and forth with the feudal lords he attempts to make see the error of their ways, (key word: attempts) Tsugumo has a constant mystery about himself which slowly unfolds in captivating fashion. Who is he? Why is he here? What is his connection to the previous Ronin who came here, Motome Chijiiwa? As each question is answered, layers upon layers of depth are added to the story. The tale of Tsugumo’s family is a tragic and painful one, reflecting on institutional corruption and the challenges of poverty, which are messages that still remain relevant today. The present has no future to live for, in a world where those in power are obsessed with the past. Allow me to also give an entire paragraph of its own to this movie’s exploration of honour. It breaks the traditional, glamourised views on Samurai honour, and instead proposes a haunting realism. The “honour” which the feudal lords attach to is nothing but, as Tsugumo himself says, a facade. It is something convenient they can hide behind, and use to benefit solely themselves. Honour on an institutional, societally ingrained level is a ridiculous prospect. It becomes little more than a tool of power, weaponising people’s own hearts and desires for good or justice against them. Note also how they only respect honour or heroism when the person is dead: there is no room for living goodness in such an oppressive and corrupt society, which benefits off of its own creation of despair and desperation, and erosion of goodwill. But honour on an individual level, is an immeasurable virtue. The depth of one’s heart, one’s mind, cannot be determined by stature or position within society. All people have it within them the ability to do good deeds of their own kind, impossible to quantify by any traditional metric. Sometimes, the right thing to do is looked down upon as weak or craven. But it is still the right thing to do. To go against the powerful and stand up as an individual is perhaps the bravest and most virtuous act one can do, even if they are discouraged from doing it. To me, this is the perfect movie. Masterfully plotted and richly detailed story, some of the finest cinematography I’ve ever witnessed, (seriously, that cinematographer better have lived like a damn monarch after this movie) and a tremendous cast who each give their all in some very memorable performances. It’s a movie where you don’t want to miss a single second, a real masterpiece. As you can probably tell, I’m quite a big fan of this one.

Lists: Top 50 Greatest Films • Greateat Historical Films • Greatest Films of the 1960’s • ————————————————————————- | Tier 5/5 — Masterpiece | As both my first Kobayashi film and the highest-rated film on Letterboxd, Harakiri came with enormous expectations, and it didn’t disappoint on either. Harakiri is so much more than a condemnation of samurai honor. At its heart is an extraordinarily moving personal tragedy about a man who watches everything he loves disappear, until all he has left is the ability to confront those responsible. The gradual revelation of Motome’s circumstances transforms what initially appears to be an act of dishonor into an act of profound love. He sells his swords, the very symbols of his identity, to care for his family, only to have that sacrifice become the instrument of his horrific death. Kobayashi makes this devastating through the way he structures the story, allowing us to witness the cruelty before revealing the tenderness and desperation behind it. The domestic scenes establish a family whose desires are painfully modest, people who simply want to survive and remain together. By the time Hanshirō confronts the clan, there is nothing left for him to save. Beneath all the political implications, this is already a masterfully constructed tragedy of love, grief, and irreversible loss. What makes the film even greater is how naturally that intimate suffering opens onto something almost archetypal about human experience. Its critique is not simply that samurai who preach honor are hypocrites, but that human beings can become so devoted to their conception of virtue that they lose the ability to recognize genuine goodness. The clan obeys its principles while committing an atrocity against someone whose supposed dishonor arose from fulfilling his most basic human responsibilities. There is also something deeply disturbing in the way the ruling order helps create the desperation it subsequently condemns. The displaced samurai are deprived of their livelihoods and then punished for the measures they take to survive. The same pattern can be recognized in empires that destabilize other nations and subsequently criminalize those driven to seek refuge within their borders. The circumstances are obviously different, but the underlying moral contradiction is remarkably similar, those who benefit from an order that produces suffering can present themselves as righteous when punishing its victims. The film reaches beyond its historical setting because it captures this recurring relationship between power, survival, and moral judgment without needing to explicitly address every form it might take. None of this depth would mean nearly as much without the precision of the filmmaking. The courtyard confrontation is an extraordinary piece of dramatic construction, with Hanshirō gradually taking control of a situation in which he initially appears completely powerless. Each revelation changes our understanding of what came before while shifting the balance of power in the present. The rigid compositions and ceremonial order of the clan give physical expression to an authority that seems immovable, making its eventual disruption all the more powerful. Yet the ending is what elevates the film into something truly extraordinary. After Hanshirō exposes the truth, the clan simply restores its armor, conceals its humiliation, and preserves its reputation through a falsified account. The institution survives not by disproving anything he has revealed, but by controlling what will be remembered. What began as a struggle to make a family’s suffering understood ends with that suffering being deliberately erased. On a personal level, this denies Hanshirō even the consolation that his final act will be acknowledged. On a larger level, it confronts the terrifying possibility that truth and moral courage may be insufficient against institutions with the power to determine history. There is a simplicity to Harakiri that makes its achievement all the more remarkable. It does not depend on exceptionally intricate psychology or endless philosophical ambiguity to achieve profundity. Like the greatest archetypal tragedies, it takes elemental experiences, love, loss, injustice, helplessness, and the need to have one’s suffering recognized, and gives them an extraordinarily powerful dramatic form. Its universal significance is not something imposed upon the story through interpretation; it emerges from the specific circumstances of these characters and the consequences of their choices. Even without considering any of its broader meanings, the film remains a devastating account of a family destroyed and a man who cannot bring them back. Yet those same events illuminate moral and political contradictions extending far beyond feudal Japan. The personal tragedy and the archetypal depth are not competing achievements, nor does either need the other to disguise its shortcomings. They are realized together with such emotional force and structural precision that Harakiri deserves consideration not only among the greatest films, but among the greatest works of tragic art.
